doc.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023

title: Cannonball and Nat Adderley at North Texas; Joe Wilder and Don Jacoby
summary: Marini's chart 'Codify' impressed Cannonball at North Texas; later friendship, and stories of Joe Wilder and Don Jacoby.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: You know you don’t hear Cannonball so much but I was very lucky — we went to hear Cannonball in Dallas when I was in North Texas and it was when I was first writing. And I wrote a chart called “Codify” which is an abstract sort of 13-bar blues. And we had a great band and Cannonball, I remember that he — of course I don’t remember anything melodically about what he played but I remember he played “Carnival” and he played like 13 choruses. And I had tears in my eyes at the end of it you know. And we went up and talked to him and Nat afterwards and we told them about North Texas, and they came

up. They came up to the school the following day. And so everybody was thrilled and Leon Breedon says, “This is a new chart by Lou Marini.” And we played the chart and when we finished it I looked up and everybody in the band was looking at me. And at first I was like what’s going on. And then I realized that Cannonball and Nat are standing right behind me over my shoulders, and Cannonball leans over to me and he says, “Lou, you a crazy motherfucker.” And you know we became friends. And I ran into him like with Woody Herman’s band, one time we were on a festival together and he comes into the dressing room in a panic, he says, “Lou, there’s something wrong with my soprano.” And I said, “Cannon, I’m not a repairman, I don’t know what the hell to do with your soprano,” I said, “but you can play mine.” So he played my soprano on the gig you know. And various times over the years I got to hang with them and you know he’s like Joe Wilder, there’s nobody that didn’t love him. He was just the fucking greatest man. And to hear him play, his rhythm, his pop on the time and his command of the horn and his sound, it was just — and Nat too. Nat was a killer player. Joe Wilder — I had gotten to know Joe in New York and I just revered him. And when I was a kid there were these “Music Minus One” records — before the Jamey Aebersold records — and one of them had Joe Wilder on it. And I just loved his playing. And so when I met him I told him about that and you know, so we became friends. And Don Jacoby, the great trumpet player that I met on the Stan Kenton jazz clinics, my roommate was Sanborn, Keith Jarrett was there, Peter Erskine was there, Randy, so many guys that ended up playing together over the years. So Jake came up to go to the Charles Colon Jazz Conference in New York and I took him to the conference. He was staying at my pad. And one of the first people who we ran into was Joe Wilder. And you know Don Jacoby was a famous trumpet player. He was a virtuoso player. So Joe knew who he was. And I said, “Joe, this is Don Jacoby, Jake this is Joe Wilder.” And Jake says, and Jake is this little guy with the diamond and the moustache you know and burly. And Jake says, “Wait a minute, Joe Wilder the jazz trumpet player, beautiful soloist?” And Joe says, “Yeah.” And Jake grabbed him like this and kissed him on the lips. And then, you know, they were laughing and they took off and they were hanging with all these other trumpet players. But yeah, Joe Wilder was a killer.
